25.text: Koryak and Kamchadal stories of such transformations of animals are

26.text: numerous, and recall the tales of the American Indians, where the animal

27.text: almost always is simply a man covered with a skin blanket. The Chukchee

28.text: stories of animals represent them, in most cases, simply as having two

29.text: shapes, animal and anthropomorphous, interchangeable (my third stage, see

30.text: p. 278). In this they resemble the stories of the Eskimo. This agrees with

31.text: other facts which show, that, while the Chukchee folk-lore is closely connected

32.text: with that of the Eskimo, the tales of the Koryak and the Kamchadal have

33.text: a closer affinity with those of the North-Pacific Indians of America.⁵ The

34.text: Koryak admit “owners” or “masters” of localities and of classes of animals,

35.text: who are quite similar to those of the Chukchee, and, indeed, are called by
